claim: Sub-Saharan Africa could lose US$3.5 billion of economic productivity every year as a result of schistosomiasis and soil-transmitted helminthiasis.
source: Recent work has estimated that sub-Saharan Africa could lose US$3.5 billion of economic productivity every year as a result of schistosomiasis and soil-transmitted helminthiasis.
evidence: The claim is supported by a reference to recent work, indicating citation-based evidence.

claim: High coverage of piped water in the community decreased a child's risk of urogenital schistosomiasis infection eight-fold (adjusted odds ratio = 0.12, 95% CI 0.06–0.26, p<0.001).
source: High coverage of piped water in the community decreased a child's risk of urogenital schistosomiasis infection eight-fold (adjusted odds ratio = 0.12, 95% CI 0.06–0.26, p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical data from the study, including adjusted odds ratios and confidence intervals.

claim: The provision of safe water could drive levels of urogenital schistosomiasis infection to low levels of endemicity in rural African settings.
source: The provision of safe water could drive levels of urogenital schistosomiasis infection to low levels of endemicity in rural African settings.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the study's findings about the impact of piped water on infection rates.

claim: Approximately 240 million people worldwide are infected with schistosomiasis.
source: Approximately, 240 million people worldwide (WHO, 2010; Stothard et al., 2009) are infected with schistosomiasis
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to WHO and Stothard et al.

claim: Schistosomiasis has a disease burden of 3.3 million disability-adjusted life-years.
source: with a disease burden of 3.3 million disability-adjusted life-years (Murray et al., 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Murray et al., 2012.

claim: In sub-Saharan Africa alone, an estimated 163 million people were infected with schistosomiasis in 2012.
source: In sub-Saharan Africa alone, an estimated 163 million people were infected in 2012 (Lai et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lai et al., 2015.

claim: The World Health Organization has set a goal of increasing mass drug administration coverage to 75% of at-risk children in endemic countries.
source: the World Health Organization (WHO) has set a goal of increasing mass drug administration coverage to 75% of at-risk children in endemic countries (WHO, 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to WHO, 2013.

claim: Schistosomiasis has the lowest coverage of all helminth diseases treatable by mass drug administration.
source: the fourth progress report of the London Declaration records that schistosomiasis has the lowest coverage of all helminth diseases treatable by mass drug administration (Uniting to Combat Neglected Tropical Diseases, 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to the fourth progress report of the London Declaration.

claim: For achieving sustained control, elimination, or eradication of schistosomiasis, improvements of water, sanitation, and hygiene infrastructure and modification of risk behaviour are necessary.
source: For achieving sustained control, elimination, or eradication of schistosomiasis, improvements of water, sanitation, and hygiene infrastructure and modification of risk behaviour are necessary (Freeman et al., 2013; WHO, 2015; Steinmann et al., 2006; Echazú et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to Freeman et al., WHO, Steinmann et al., and Echazú et al.

claim: Previous studies on the impact of provision of safe water on schistosomiasis infection were of poor quality and likely confounded by multiple socio-economic and other variables.
source: Recently, a systematic review concluded that previous studies on this topic were of poor quality and likely confounded by multiple socio-economic and other variables (Grimes et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a systematic review by Grimes et al., 2014.

claim: The introduction of safe water supplies into a community offers direct protection to individuals with access to safe water by reducing their contact with infected water bodies.
source: Firstly, it offers direct protection to individuals with access to safe water by reducing their contact with infected water bodies through household domestic water collection activities.
evidence: The claim is based on logical inference about the mechanism of protection from safe water.

claim: The scale-up in access to safe water confers indirect protection to members of a community in a manner analogous to 'herd immunity'.
source: Secondly, the scale-up in access to safe water will confer indirect protection to members of a community in a manner that is analogous to the concept of 'herd immunity' (Fine et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Fine et al., 2011, and draws on the established concept of herd immunity.

claim: Of the 2105 participants tested in the parasitological survey, 353 were infected with Schistosoma haematobium.
source: Of the 2105 participants tested in the parasitological survey, 353 were infected with Schistosoma haematobium.
evidence: The claim is directly supported by data from the parasitological survey.

claim: The overall prevalence of Schistosoma haematobium was 16.8% (95% CI: 15.2–18.4).
source: The overall prevalence was 16.8% (95% CI: 15.2–18.4)
evidence: The claim is directly supported by data from the parasitological survey.

claim: The prevalence of heavy infection (≥50 eggs/10 ml of urine) was 9.5% (95% CI: 8.3–10.8).
source: the prevalence of heavy infection (≥50 eggs/10 ml of urine) was 9.5% (95% CI: 8.3–10.8)
evidence: The claim is directly supported by data from the parasitological survey.

claim: Prevalence of Schistosoma haematobium was twice as high in boys compared to girls (22.6% versus 11.4%).
source: Prevalence was twice as high in boys compared to girls (22.6% versus 11.4%)
evidence: The claim is directly supported by data from the parasitological survey.

claim: Prevalence of Schistosoma haematobium peaked at 30% in boys at age 14 years.
source: peaked at 30% in boys at age 14 years
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the text and Figure 1.

claim: Prevalence of Schistosoma haematobium peaked at 15% in girls at age 12 years.
source: 15% in girls at age 12 years (Figure 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the text and Figure 1.

claim: 57% of all infected participants had heavy infections with a geometric mean egg burden of 65 eggs/10 ml urine.
source: 57% of all infected participants had heavy infections with a geometric mean egg burden of 65 eggs/10 ml urine.
evidence: The claim is directly supported by data from the parasitological survey.

claim: 80% of the egg burden was borne by just 3.4% of all pupils tested (20.4% of all infected participants).
source: Overall, 80% of the egg burden was borne by just 3.4% of all pupils tested (20.4% of all infected participants).
evidence: The claim is directly supported by data from the parasitological survey.

claim: 67% of participants who were present at school on the day of testing had parental consent and assent and provided a urine specimen.
source: Overall, 67% of participants who were present at school on the day of testing had parental consent and assent and provided a urine specimen.
evidence: The claim is directly supported by data from the study.

claim: Only 2.2% of linked participants reported receiving praziquantel in the last 12 months.
source: Only 2.2% of linked participants reported receiving praziquantel in the last 12 months (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the text and Table 1.

claim: The kernel-derived prevalence of urogenital schistosomiasis varied between 0% and 85%.
source: The kernel-derived prevalence of urogenital schistosomiasis varied between 0% and 85%
evidence: The claim is directly supported by data from the geospatial analysis.

claim: Four significant foci of Schistosoma haematobium infection were identified around open water collection sites (relative risk = 2.99–5.63, p<0.05).
source: A formal micro-geographical clustering analysis using the Kulldorff spatial scan statistic revealed four significant foci of infection around open water collection sites (relative risk = 2.99–5.63, p<0.05; Figure 2, Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the Kulldorff spatial scan statistic analysis, presented in text, Figure 2, and Table 2.

claim: Between 2001 and 2007, the provision of piped water in the surveillance area nearly doubled from 42% to 80%.
source: Between 2001 and 2007, the provision of piped water in the surveillance area nearly doubled from 42% to 80% (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the text and Figure 3.

claim: The community-based mean coverage of piped water between 2001 and 2007 was 61.7%.
source: The community-based mean coverage of piped water between 2001 and 2007 was 61.7% (Figure 3, bottom right).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the text and Figure 3.

claim: Participants living in communities with a high coverage of piped water (median coverage = 95.5%) were eight times less likely to be infected (aOR = 0.12, 95% CI 0.06–0.26, p<0.001) in comparison to those living in communities with lowest coverage (median coverage = 8.4%).
source: Participants living in communities with a high coverage of piped water (median coverage = 95.5%) were eight times less likely to be infected (aOR = 0.12, 95% CI 0.06–0.26, p<0.001; Model 1 of Table 3) in comparison to those living in communities with lowest coverage (median coverage = 8.4%).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical data from the study, presented in text and Table 3.

claim: Household access to piped water was independently associated with a significant reduction in the odds of infection (aOR = 0.54, 95% CI: 0.33–0.89, p=0.017).
source: We found that this exposure was independently associated with a significant reduction in the odds of infection (aOR = 0.54, 95% CI: 0.33–0.89, p=0.017; Model 2 of Table 3)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical data from the study, presented in text and Table 3.

claim: The reduction in risk from household piped water was driven mostly by the reduction in risk in girls (aOR = 0.38, 95% CI: 0.19–0.75, p=0.005).
source: Once again this reduction was driven mostly by the reduction in risk in girls (aOR = 0.38, 95% CI: 0.19–0.75, p=0.005; Model 2 of Table 4)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical data from the study, presented in text and Table 4.

claim: The reduction in risk from household piped water in boys was not statistically significant (aOR = 0.76, 95% CI: 0.41–1.42, p=0.38).
source: which was substantially larger than the corresponding impact in boys (aOR = 0.76, 95% CI: 0.41–1.42, p=0.38; Model 2 of Table 4, see also Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical data from the study, presented in text, Table 4, and Figure 5.

claim: The risk-reduction estimate for access to piped water at the household level (aOR = 0.54) is close to the Schistosoma haematobium specific aOR of 0.57 generated as part of Grimes et al. systematic review.
source: Our risk-reduction estimate for access to piped water at the household level (aOR = 0.54) is close to the Schistosoma haematobium specific aOR of 0.57 generated as part of Grimes et al. systematic review (Grimes et al., 2014) comprising 17 previous studies (Abou-Zeid et al., 2012; Al-Waleedi et al., 2013; Awoke et al., 2013; Dame et al., 2006; Dawet, 2012; Farooq et al., 1966; Howarth et al., 1988; Knopp et al., 2013; Nworie et al., 2012; Reuben et al., 2013; Sady et al., 2013) (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with data from a systematic review and meta-analysis.

claim: The instrumental variable met the relevance condition of instrumental variable estimation, as shown by the size of the F-test for instrument strength (F-statistic = 55).
source: Our instrumental variable met the relevance condition of instrumental variable estimation, as shown by the size of the F-test for instrument strength (F-statistic = 55).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical data from the instrumental variable analysis.

claim: In the IV analysis using a linear model, a 1% increase in the coverage of piped water in the surrounding community was independently associated with a 0.48% decrease in the risk of urogenital schistosomiasis infection (Coef= –0.0048, p<0.001).
source: In the IV analysis using a linear model, a 1% increase in the coverage of piped water in the surrounding community was independently associated with a 0.48% decrease in the risk of urogenital schistosomiasis infection (Coef= –0.0048, p<0.001; Model 2 of Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical data from the instrumental variable analysis.

claim: Household access to piped water was associated with a 15.6% reduction in the risk of infection in the IV analysis (Coef = –0.156, p=0.035).
source: Household access to piped water was associated with a 15.6% reduction in the risk of infection (Coef = –0.156, p=0.035; Model 4 of Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical data from the instrumental variable analysis.

claim: Nearly 1 in 5 primary school children (median age = 11 years) were infected with urogenital schistosomiasis.
source: Our results show that nearly 1 in 5 primary school children (median age = 11 years) were infected with urogenital schistosomiasis
evidence: The claim is directly supported by data from the parasitological survey.

claim: Nearly 1 in 10 primary school children were heavily infected with urogenital schistosomiasis.
source: nearly 1 in 10 were heavily infected
evidence: The claim is directly supported by data from the parasitological survey.

claim: These levels of urogenital schistosomiasis infection are markedly lower than the overall prevalence of 60–70% recorded in the general area thirty years earlier.
source: These levels of urogenital schistosomiasis infection are markedly lower than the overall prevalence of 60–70% recorded in the general area thirty years earlier (Gear et al., 1980)
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with historical data cited from Gear et al., 1980.

claim: The prevalence of urogenital schistosomiasis was 69% in a recent survey undertaken in a neighbouring district at similar altitude (<300 metres above sea level) but with limited access to piped water.
source: 69% prevalence recorded in a more recent survey undertaken in a neighbouring district at similar altitude (<300 metres above sea level) but with limited access to piped water (Saathoff et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by data cited from Saathoff et al., 2004.

claim: The prevalence of infection was >80% in some communities where the roll-out of piped water had not taken place.
source: For example, the prevalence of infection was >80% in some communities where the roll-out of piped water had not taken place.
evidence: The claim is directly supported by data from the study.

claim: Boys had more than twice the prevalence of urogenital schistosomiasis infection in comparison to girls.
source: Another important finding to emerge from the work is that the greater burden of urogenital schistosomiasis infection is borne by boys who had more than twice the prevalence of infection in comparison to girls.
evidence: The claim is directly supported by data from the study.

claim: Higher socio-economic status was independently associated with a decrease in the odds of infection for girls but not for boys.
source: Whilst environmental variables (distance to water-body, altitude and landcover class) were highly predictive of infection in both sexes, higher socio-economic status was independently associated with a decrease in the odds of infection for girls but not for boys.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: At the community level, piped water coverage was associated with significantly greater reductions in the infection risk for girls.
source: At the community level, piped water coverage was associated with significantly greater reductions in the infection risk for girls.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Household access to piped water was associated with a significant reduction in risk in girls but not in boys.
source: Similarly, household access to piped water was associated with a significant reduction in risk in girls but not in boys.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: The sex differences at both the community and household level could reflect the cultural context in which girls are responsible for the majority of the domestic water collection and/or a situation where boys swim more often in infected water bodies.
source: These sex differences at both the community and household level could reflect the cultural context in which girls are responsible for the majority of the domestic water collection and/or a situation where boys swim more often in infected water bodies (Ngorima et al., 2008; Thomassen Morgas et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference and supported by citations to Ngorima et al., 2008 and Thomassen Morgas et al., 2010.

claim: The greater than four-fold ratio in the community-level (aOR = 0.12) versus household-level (aOR = 0.54) risk-reduction estimate provides empirical support for the viewpoint that it is crucial to look beyond the household and consider the piped water coverage level in the surrounding local community.
source: The greater than four-fold ratio in the community-level (aOR = 0.12) versus household-level (aOR = 0.54) risk-reduction estimate provides empirical support for this viewpoint.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the comparison of two effect-size estimates from the study.

claim: A study in China found Schistosoma japonicum infection rates to be significantly lower in communities where more than 50% of people used 'hygienic lavatories'.
source: Whilst no such community-level analyses have previously been conducted for Schistosoma haematobium, a study in China found Schistosoma japonicum infection rates to be significantly lower in communities where more than 50% of people used 'hygienic lavatories' (Yang et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yang et al., 2009.

claim: The study design overcomes many of the limitations typically associated with school-based surveys in which the exposures and disease outcomes are measured at the same point in time.
source: Our study design has several strengths that overcome many of the limitations typically associated with school-based surveys in which the exposures and disease outcomes are measured at the same point in time.
evidence: The claim is based on inference about the study design's advantages.

claim: The results are based on a single urine sample and as a result the study would likely have missed some light infections.
source: The results are based on a single urine sample and as a result we would likely have missed some light infections (Kosinski et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is based on inference about the limitations of single urine sampling, supported by a citation to Kosinski et al., 2011.

claim: The true prevalence of infection is probably higher than 16.8% reported in this study.
source: The true prevalence of infection is therefore probably higher than 16.8% reported in this study.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the limitation of single urine sampling.

claim: South Africa is a country with near-universal primary school attendance.
source: A further limitation is that, while South Africa is a country with near-universal primary school attendance (Lund, 2011)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lund, 2011.

claim: Schistosomiasis and soil-transmitted helminthiasis affect more than 1.5 billion of the world's poorest people.
source: Schistosomiasis and soil-transmitted helminthiasis affect more than 1.5 billion of the world's poorest people (Lai et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lai et al., 2015.

claim: Without a change in strategy to control these diseases, the population of sub-Saharan Africa will lose an estimated US$3.5 billion of economic productivity every year, which is comparable to recent acute epidemics, including the 2014 Ebola and 2015 Zika epidemics.
source: Without a change in strategy to control these diseases, the population of sub-Saharan Africa will lose an estimated US$3.5 billion of economic productivity every year, which is comparable to recent acute epidemics, including the 2014 Ebola and 2015 Zika epidemics (Lo et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lo et al., 2017.

claim: Recent modelling work indicates that the current WHO treatment goals (which aim to mass-treat 75% of at-risk children) should be successful in eradicating schistosomiasis transmission if continued for a decade in areas of low to moderate transmission.
source: Recent modelling work indicates that the current WHO treatment goals (which aim to mass-treat 75% of at-risk children) should be successful in eradicating schistosomiasis transmission if continued for a decade in areas of low to moderate transmission (Anderson et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Anderson et al., 2015.

claim: Once mass treatment is suspended, the prevalence of infection can rebound to pre-control levels over a period of 25–30 years.
source: However, once mass treatment is suspended, the prevalence of infection can rebound to pre-control levels over a period of 25–30 years (Gurarie et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gurarie et al., 2015.

claim: The overall moderate levels of infection combined with the extreme inter-host and geographical heterogeneity as well as ever increasing access to safe water suggest that sustained mass treatment campaigns in such populations could drive schistosomiasis towards low levels of endemicity.
source: The overall moderate levels of infection (significantly lower than historical surveys (Gear et al., 1980) combined with the extreme inter-host and geographical heterogeneity as well as ever increasing access to safe water suggest that sustained mass treatment campaigns in such populations could drive schistosomiasis towards low levels of endemicity (Crompton and WHO, 2006).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the study's findings and supported by citations.

claim: In South Africa, Schistosoma haematobium is endemic over an area of 320 000 km2 including parts of six of the country's nine provinces to the east of latitude 26°E.
source: In South Africa, Schistosoma haematobium is endemic over an area of 320 000 km2 including parts of six of the country's nine provinces to the east of latitude 26°E (Doumenge et al., 1987).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Doumenge et al., 1987.

claim: Highest prevalence and intensities of Schistosoma haematobium occur in the lower lying areas of Limpopo, Mpumalanga and KwaZulu-Natal provinces.
source: Highest prevalence and intensities occur in the lower lying areas of Limpopo, Mpumalanga and KwaZulu-Natal provinces.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about schistosomiasis distribution in South Africa.

claim: Estimates of the number of children infected with Schistosoma haematobium in South Africa range from 1.5 million to 4 million.
source: Estimates of the number of children infected have been based largely on the 38 year old Atlas of Bilharzia (Gear et al., 1980), and range from 1.5 million to 4 million (Moodley et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gear et al., 1980 and Moodley et al., 2003.

claim: The most frequently infected age group with Schistosoma haematobium is 5 to 15 years after which prevalence declines to a generally low level in adulthood.
source: The most frequently infected age group is 5 to 15 years after which prevalence declines to a generally low level in adulthood.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about schistosomiasis epidemiology.

claim: Considerable gynaecological morbidity, also due to Schistosoma haematobium and known as female genital schistosomiasis, has been demonstrated in KwaZulu-Natal.
source: Considerable gynaecological morbidity, also due to Schistosoma haematobium and known as female genital schistosomiasis, has been demonstrated in KwaZulu-Natal (Hegertun et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hegertun et al., 2013.

claim: Schistosoma haematobium has a significantly wider distribution in South Africa than its congener Schistosoma mansoni which causes intestinal or rectal schistosomiasis.
source: Schistosoma haematobium has a significantly wider distribution in South Africa than its congener Schistosoma mansoni which causes intestinal or rectal schistosomiasis (Appleton and Madsen, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Appleton and Madsen, 2012.

claim: Historically Schistosoma haematobium prevalence and intensities have reached 70% or more and 200 eggs/10 ml (geometric mean) respectively between the coast and an altitude of 300 meters above sea level in KwaZulu-Natal.
source: KwaZulu-Natal is the best researched of the endemic provinces in South Africa and historically Schistosoma haematobium prevalence and intensities have reached 70% or more and 200 eggs/10 ml (geometric mean) respectively between the coast and an altitude of 300 meters above sea level.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about historical schistosomiasis prevalence in KwaZulu-Natal.

claim: Both prevalence and intensity of Schistosoma haematobium have been observed to decrease with increasing altitude to around 20% and <10 eggs/10 ml above 800 metres above sea level.
source: Both prevalence and intensity have been observed to decrease with increasing altitude to around 20% and <10 eggs/10 ml above 800 metres above sea level.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the relationship between altitude and schistosomiasis.

claim: Schistosoma mansoni is less common and limited to patches of transmission, mostly in KwaZulu-Natal's lowlands.
source: Schistosoma mansoni is less common and limited to patches of transmission, mostly in the province's lowlands (Appleton and Kvalsvig, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Appleton and Kvalsvig, 2006.

claim: In the coastal plain of north-eastern KwaZulu-Natal (where the survey was conducted), Schistosoma mansoni is largely absent.
source: In the coastal plain of north-eastern KwaZulu-Natal (where the survey was conducted), Schistosoma mansoni is largely absent (Gear et al., 1980)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gear et al., 1980.

claim: The Africa Health Research Institute (AHRI) runs one of Africa's largest ongoing population-based cohorts in the Umkhanyakude district of the northern KwaZulu-Natal province.
source: The Africa Health Research Institute (AHRI) runs one of Africa's largest ongoing population-based cohorts in the Umkhanyakude district of the northern KwaZulu-Natal province (Figure 7).
evidence: The claim is a factual statement about the study setting.

claim: The surveillance area is 438 km2 in size with a population of approximately 90,000 isiZulu-speaking people and 10,000 households.
source: the surveillance area is 438 km2 in size with a population of approximately 90,000 isiZulu-speaking people and 10,000 households.
evidence: The claim is a factual statement about the study setting.

claim: AHRI has collected detailed demographic, socio-economic and behavioural data every four to six months from residents in the surveillance area since 2000.
source: AHRI has collected detailed demographic, socio-economic and behavioural data every four to six months from residents in the surveillance area since 2000 (Tanser et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tanser et al., 2008.

claim: All households have been positioned to an accuracy of <2 m using differential global positioning systems.
source: All households have been positioned to an accuracy of <2 m using differential global positioning systems (Tanser et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tanser et al., 2001.

claim: The surveillance area is designated as a coastal lowland (<300 metres above sea level) and falls within the endemic schistosomiasis belt of South Africa.
source: The surveillance area is designated as a coastal lowland (<300 metres above sea level) and falls within the endemic schistosomiasis belt of South Africa (Gear et al., 1980; Moodley et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gear et al., 1980 and Moodley et al., 2003.

claim: In 2010, the HIV prevalence was 24% among all adults in the surveillance area.
source: In 2010, the HIV prevalence was 24% among all adults
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Tanser et al., 2013 and Vandormael et al., 2018.

claim: In 2010, HIV prevalence was approaching 60% in some age-groups in the surveillance area.
source: approaching 60% in some age-groups (Tanser et al., 2013; Vandormael et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Tanser et al., 2013 and Vandormael et al., 2018.

claim: A parasitological survey was conducted among 2105 consenting children (median age = 11) in their fifth and sixth year of primary school at all of the 33 primary schools in the surveillance area between March and December 2007.
source: We conducted a parasitological survey among 2105 consenting children (median age = 11) in their fifth and sixth year of primary school at all of the 33 primary schools in the surveillance area between March and December 2007.
evidence: The claim is a factual statement about the study methods.

claim: 94% (N = 1,976) of children who participated in the parasitological survey could be linked to their corresponding records in the population-based cohort.
source: Of the 2105 children who participated in our parasitological survey, 94% (N = 1,976) could be linked to their corresponding records in the population-based cohort and were included in the statistical analysis.
evidence: The claim is directly supported by data from the study.

claim: The reduction in risk from household piped water was significantly greater for girls (p=0.014).
source: When formally testing this as an interaction effect in the combined-sex model, the reduction in risk was significantly greater for girls (p=0.014).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: A piped water coverage of 30% would correspond to a greater than 50% decrease in the odds of infection for individuals living in that community.
source: For example, a piped water coverage of 30% would correspond to a greater than 50% decrease in the odds of infection for individuals living in that community (Figure 4b).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the non-linear relationship shown in Figure 4b.

claim: When the size of the kernel's search radius was increased from 2 km to 3 km, the continuous effect-size estimate remained virtually unchanged (aOR = 0.97, 95% CI: 0.96–0.98, p<0.001).
source: For example, when we increased the size of the kernel's search radius from 2 km to 3 km then we found that both the continuous (aOR = 0.97, 95% CI: 0.96–0.98, p<0.001)
evidence: The claim is supported by sensitivity analysis data.

claim: When the size of the kernel's search radius was increased from 2 km to 3 km, the categorical effect-size estimate remained virtually unchanged (quintile five versus quintile one aOR = 0.12, 95% CI: 0.06–0.24, p<0.001).
source: and categorical effect-size estimates (quintile five versus quintile one aOR = 0.12, 95% CI: 0.06–0.24, p<0.001) remained virtually unchanged.
evidence: The claim is supported by sensitivity analysis data.

claim: When piped water coverage only in the year of the parasitological survey (2007) was used, the resulting risk-reduction was attenuated (by 44%) but nevertheless still significant (aOR = 0.986, 95% CI: 0.98–0.99, p=0.004).
source: For a comparative exercise, we replaced the mean community-level piped water exposure (2001–2007) exposure variable with the piped water coverage only in the year of the parasitological survey (2007). As anticipated, we find in this model that the resulting risk-reduction is attenuated (by 44%) but nevertheless still significant (aOR = 0.986, 95% CI: 0.98–0.99, p=0.004)
evidence: The claim is supported by sensitivity analysis data.
